source.title: GNU Grep Manual, §2.3 Exit Status
source.quote: Normally the exit status is 0 if a line is selected, 1 if no lines were selected, and 2 if an error occurred.

support_assessment.strong_claim: exit 2 = could not evaluate, distinct from exit 1 = answer is no
caveats: manual says 'an error occurred', not literally 'could not evaluate' — the gate reading is interpretive but faithful
-q/--quiet/--silent carve-out: exit 0 with a selected line even if an error occurred; a strict gate must not copy that precedence
no refusal code exists in grep's 0/1/2 map; the registry row's refusal cell is the lane's own design (sysexits(3) would be the grounding candidate, not fetched — one-source scope)
'Other grep implementations may exit with status greater than 2 on error' — 2 is grep's convention, not universal
support_assessment.weak_claim_supported: exit codes are a documented contract (trivially, yes)

sources_check.proposed_scope: GNU grep's own documented exit-status contract for a predicate program (0 selected / 1 none / 2 trouble)
